name: eagle

attributes.attribute: a symbolic bird weak in power but used to mark completeness in identity lists
an ancient invader who took the eagle among his many forms
a magical pig that gave birth to eaglets, bees and wolves
the Welsh hero whose sole form was the eagle
where eagles were held to be oracular and control the weather

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The eagle is a symbolic bird. This large bird of prey was once plentiful in Celtic lands. Now it is far less so. Its size and fierceness did not give it much symbolic power among the Celts. They used the eagle mainly to show completeness in a list of a figure's other identities. The one-eyed salmon of wisdom could appear as Fintan. That ancient invader shifted into many forms, the eagle among them. In British legend a magic pig named Henwen bore eaglets and also made bees and wolves. Only the hero Lleu Llaw Gyffes took the eagle for himself. He changed into it after his wife murdered him. The bird sometimes marked oracles or came as an omen of things to come. A shape-shifting magician or bard could also wear the eagle's form. Other lore kept a belief in the eagle's might. In Wales the birds held the power of divination. Eagles on Mount Snowdon were held to be oracular. They could control the weather. People who ate eagle flesh gave their heirs strong psychic powers. These lasted to the ninth generation.

okr.objective: Describe the eagle as a Celtic symbolic bird with limited power but strong mythic reach.
key_results: The eagle once was plentiful in Celtic lands and now is far less so.
The Celts used the eagle to show completeness in identity lists, not for power.
Myth links the eagle to Fintan, to Henwen's eaglets, and to Lleu Llaw Gyffes.
In Wales eagles on Mount Snowdon were oracular and could control the weather.
